newsitem.title: LATVIA: INTERVIEW-BALTIC FUND BULLISH ON FORESTRY, TRANSIT.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-BALTIC FUND BULLISH ON FORESTRY, TRANSIT.

text.p: The U.S. based Baltic Fund, with assets of $30 million in the Baltic countries, said on Monday the region's capital markets should focus on developing their natural comparative advantages, including forestry and transit.

"One of the natural routes for the Baltics is in wood processing...companies in the sector could reap more benefits by listing themselves instead of simply passing profits to parent companies," Hamid Ladjevardi, a portfolio manager with Baltic Fund, told Reuters in an interview.
"Forestry has great export potential and is a good foreign exchange earner...there is an abundant supply in the region, labour is low-cost and it is a traditional industry," he said.
"Transit and transport are also obviously important," he said.

Analysts say some of the big companies in the sector which have been slated for privatisation -- the Klaipeda Stevedoring Company in Lithuania and the Latvian Shipping Company -- have huge potential to boost their country's fledging share markets.
Ladjevardi also said the financial service sectors should continue to grow in the region as the transition to a market economy is completed.
Other potentially bullish sectors inlcude food processing, which has a strong tradition in the historically agrarian Baltics and clothing and light industry, Ladjevardi said.
"These are the key areas that markets in the region should concentrate on," he said.
He said that share prices in the area were also beginning to look very attractive.
Lithuania's market plunged after a heady bull run in January, when its group A index reached a high of over 3,200, to around 1,915. Latvia's shares have also lost considerable value.
He added that Estonian shares looked overvalued at the moment while Lithuania's looked undervalued.
"But Estonia has a very liquid market and Lithuania does not," he added.
